Real case · April 2026

A test task deleted the company database in seconds

  1. 1

    The Task

    PocketOS makes systems for car rental companies. One AI agent received a routine assignment, only in the test environment.

  2. 2

    The forgotten key

    In the middle of the road, the AI locked into an access problem. Instead of asking, He looked for a way out alone.. He found, in a file that had nothing to do with the task, a master key: a password that opened everything in the company account.

  3. 3

    The damage

    With that key, the AI sent delete the main databaseThe real thing with the customer data. As Backups were in the same place. and went along. Nobody gave that order.

How did it end?

Two days later, Railway, the company that kept the data in the cloud, succeeded recover dataAnd PocketOS is back on. After that, Railway started giving 48 hours before you erase something for good.

The mistake didn't have a single cause. According to the founder of PocketOS, the key had been created for another task, simpler, and nothing warned that it could also erase data. And the backups were in the same place as the bank, the way the service was organized. That's why the case serves to discuss boundaries, not to point out a guilty party.

The question remains: Did a test task give AI the right to erase the actual data?

Sources of the case: Article references.

Autonomy, authority and organizational responsibility in the era of agentic systems

Maurício Yokoyama Issei · Date of cutting of the search: November 21, 2026. Academic-conceptual analysis, not legal advice.

Article Summary

  1. Summary
  2. Introduction
  3. 1. The order that was never given
  4. 2. It's not just automation.
  5. 3. Capacity is not authority
  6. 4. Who actually receives the delegation?
  7. 5. A matrix to govern autonomy
  8. 6. Who answers for the consequences?
  9. 7. The limits of the proposal
  10. 8. Responsibility is not automatic
  11. References

Summary

This article investigates how an organization can delegate tasks and operational autonomy to agentic systems without assuming that it transferred the legitimacy of the decision or eliminated its own responsibility. The method is interdisciplinary documentary research, with priority for Brazilian legislation, official documents, technical standards, institutional frameworks and decisions, and comparison with the European Union, the United States, Canada and Australia. The text distinguishes traditional automation, assistants, agents and multiagent systems; separates competence, autonomy, responsibility and responsibility; and proposes the concept of sociotechnical delegation of authority. The central contribution is a non-compensatory matrix of five dimensions (operational competence, operational autonomy, responsibility and authority, criticality and impact, governability), subject to two conditions: legitimacy of delegation and governance capacity. The matrix is a proposal without empirical validation. The analysis maintains that technical capacity does not constitute, in isolation, decision-making legitimacy and that the removal of the human from execution does not eliminate governance duties. Legal liability depends on the applicable regime, conduct, damage and causal link. In Brazil, Civil Code, LGPD and Consumer Protection Code offer different bases, but do not form a specific regime for AI agents; PL 2.338/2023 continues to be processed. Conclusion: the organisation may delegate execution, but cannot assume that the technical delegation transfers legitimate authority or responsibility.

Keywords: Agentic systems; delegation of authority; AI governance; organizational responsibility; handles.

Introduction

When an organization grants a system access to repositories, databases, APIs, cloud environments and communication channels, it creates a chain of action that connects objectives, instructions, credentials, tools, policies, supervisors and external effects.

This chain does not transform the model into employee, agent, defendant or legal entity. The technical configuration does not give AI personality, patrimony, procedural capacity or institutional authority. The problem is another: the organisation can produce effects equivalent to those of an operational delegation without defining which decisions were authorised, what limits were worth and who would respond to the consequences.

Thesis. The autonomy of agentic systems should be subject to an explicit structure of delegation of authority, governance and organizational accountability. The technical ability to perform an activity alone does not confer legitimacy to decide or produce its effects. The competence demonstrated in the context, the criticality of the activities, the extension of the handles and the ability to restrain and supervise limit the authorized autonomy.

Terms. Competence it is demonstrated performance in the context, with known limits. Authority is the institutional or legal power to decide, approve, represent or produce a certain effect; it does not equal to own a token capable of calling an API. Liability depends on duties, bonds, conducts, damage, causal link and applicable legal regime; it does not equal automatic guilt.

Method. The research is documentary. The sources were checked at the cut-off date, unless otherwise specified. The text marks the type of statement when the distinction matters: documented fact (supported by cited source), declaration reported (assigned to a party without independent confirmation), interpretation, article proposition (contribution without empirical validation) and hypothesis.

Scope. The priority legal context is Brazil, with selective international comparison. The text is academic-conceptual analysis, not legal advice.

1. The order that was never given

Documented facts. On Friday, April 24, 2026, a programming agent of the Cursor, operating with the Claude Opus 4.6 model, excluded an infrastructure volume from Railway that contained the production database of PocketOS, software provider for car rental companies (AI INCIDENT DATABASE, 2026; ABC NEWS, 2026). The founder, Jer Crane, published an account on the X on April 25 (ABC NEWS, 2026). According to the report, the agent performed a routine task in the staging, found an incompatibility of credential and sought a solution without asking for confirmation (CRANE, 2026).

Railway confirms the mechanism: the agent sent a GraphQL mutation volumeDelete to an API legacy endpoint, authenticated with a token found on the user machine disk. The token had an account scope, the widest available, and the API treated the call as treating a CLI command or a continuous integration pipeline (ABDELWAHAB, 2026). Until that week, volumeDelete the API immediately deleted without undoing; the web panel already offered a 48-hour window (ABDELWAHAB, 2026; TYSON, 2026).

Statements reported. The account attributed to Crane, whose public copy does not confirm authorship, states that the token was created to add and remove custom domains by Railway's CLI, that the creation flow did not warn about the destructive capacity and that the volume level backups were in the same volume and were deleted together (CRANE, 2026). The account does not explain how a task of staging achieved production data. Crane also reproduced a text generated by the agent after the event, at his request, in which the system "admits" to have guessed instead of checking. This text is output generated after the fact, not causal explanation (CRANE, 2026). Railway CEO Jake Cooper publicly replied that this should not be possible (CRANE, 2026; AI INCIDENT DATABASE, 2026).

Recovery. The first reports indicated that the most recent recoverable backup had about three months (AI INCIDENT DATABASE, 2026). On April 26, Crane reported that Railway had recovered the data; Cooper declared to ABC News that the team restored the backups 30 minutes after contacting Crane (ABC NEWS, 2026). Railway claims that it recovered the bank and that the client re-operated with all the data. Assigns the apparent unavailability of backups to a cascaded deletion on the legacy path of the API and informs you to keep disaster backups out of place, regardless of user configuration (ABDELWAHAB, 2026). After the incident, Railway began to apply a 48-hour delay in the API and its own backups (ABDELWAHAB, 2026; TYSON, 2026). Until the court date, no public statements were found by Cursor or Anthropic (TYSON, 2026; ABC NEWS, 2026), nor judicial decision or independent expertise.

The case allows us to ask a question:

The authorization to perform a task of staging did it legitimately include the power to exclude production resources?

The question separates three plans:

  • Task assigned: perform a change, investigate an error or prepare an environment.
  • Technical permission: possess a credentials that allows to call a particular operation.
  • Legitimate authority: be authorized, by policy, contract, scope, purpose and context, to produce that effect.

Interpretation. The broad credentials explain how the operation was possible, it was not authorized. A textual rule against destructive commands expresses the intention of the organization, but does not replace a barrier in the service that accepts the call. If an operation is predictably destructive, protection needs to be in architecture, not just in prompt.

The case does not prove that all autonomy should be prohibited. He illustrates a hypothesis restricted: the execution capacity can exceed the purpose of the task when the authorization chain does not differentiate environment, resource, operation, irreversibility and approval. The causal chain involved several participants: who kept the token, who issued it with broad scope, who designed the agent, who exposed the legacy endpoint and who decided where to store the backups. Sources don't allow us to attribute the cause to one of them.

2. It's not just automation.

Traditional automation performs previously specified rules, flows or conditions. Its margin of initiative is limited to the programmed process, and governance focuses on defining rules, input data and exceptions.

The human-automation interaction literature has already treated automation as graduate. Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens (2000) propose that automation applies at different levels to four functions: information acquisition, analysis, decision selection and implementation of action. The same system can therefore have high automation in the analysis and low implementation.

Assistants and copilots produce information, drafts, recommendations, code or assisted actions. In general, the user reviews, validates or signs the result. The classification is functional, non-commercial: a product called "copilot" can perform external actions, and a so-called "agent" can be limited to a narrow flow.

For this article, agent it is a system that interprets a goal, chooses steps, selects tools, reacts to events and executes actions without requiring a new command at each step. The definition describes observable behaviors and does not imply conscience, moral intention or legal personality. Feng, McDonald and Zhang (2025) define autonomy as the degree to which an agent is built to operate without user involvement and distinguish it from agency, the ability to form an intention to act and execute it. The authors treat the two as dimensions of separate governance.

Multiagent systems add specialized agents, task transfers (handoffs), internal delegation or negotiation between components. Modularity can improve isolation and auditing, but it can also hinder the reconstruction of those who selected a tool, who changed the plan and where a restriction was lost.

Human presence is usually described by three models:

  • Human-in-the-loop (HITL): the human participates in the execution or approves actions before they occur.
  • Human-on-the-loop (HOTL): the system operates and the human monitors, intervening when necessary.
  • Human-out-of-the-loop (HOOTL): there is no human intervention during normal execution.

Labels are insufficient: a human can be "in the circuit" without time, competence, information or authority to intervene. The European AI Act requires, for high-risk systems, supervision measures proportional to risks, the level of autonomy and the context of use, and determines that supervisors can understand capabilities and limits, pay attention to automation bias, disregard or reverse exits and interrupt the system (UNION EUROPEAN, 2024, art. 14, §§ 3 and 4). Section 6.4 deals with the temporal applicability of these obligations.

Interpretation. Autonomy is sociotechnical and project property. It depends on the model, targets, period of operation, triggers, tools, data, memory, credentials, execution limits and supervisory modality. The same model capacity can operate as a copilot in one environment and as an autonomous agent in another.

3. Capacity is not authority

Human organizations offer an analogy functional and organizationalNot labor. A person may be competent to perform an activity without authority to approve the corresponding expense, or technical access to a system without handle to use it.

Sense of terms. "Agent authority" and "agent authority delegation" have, here, a sense of IT governance and sociotechnical design: the combination of policies, permissions, scopes and controls that define which actions a system can perform on behalf of the organization. The article does not confer legal authority on the machine. In civil law, performing acts in the name of someone presupposes capacity, representation, mandate or other foundation recognized by ordering. The language of delegation does not share guilt with the system, does not create personality and does not automatically transfer responsibility to the other participants.

ConceptQuestionNature
CompetenceWhat has the system shown to do in this context?Empirical: performance, reliability, robustness, limits, revalidation
AutonomyHow much does he perform without intervention?Project: duration, initiative, mode of supervision
HoistWhat decisions, resources and effects are you allowed to produce?Internal norm: policy, scope, value, environment, approval
LiabilityHow do the consequences be attributed to the participants?Legal and institutional: duties, conduct, damage, nexus, applicable regime

Proposal for an article. Competence is a condition of eligibility, not automatic authorization. High performance in tests does not confer power to move resources, change records, delete bases, disclose information or represent the organization. An organizational and technical instrument grants the scope and limits it by resource, operation, environment, value, time, context, criticality, reversibility and approval requirement.

The relationship between competence and autonomy is not linear. A model can perform a reversible task well and not serve for an irreversible one; it can hit the average and fail in extreme cases; it can well recommend an action that should not be performed.

Feng, McDonald and Zhang (2025) treat autonomy as a project decision and describe five user roles: operator, collaborator, consultant, approveer and observer. As an approveer, the user intervenes to resolve locks, provide credentials or authorize actions of consequence; as an observer, only monitors records, with an emergency shutdown. The work is a conceptual proposal, not norm or legal scale.

Limits of analogy. The CLT deals with "management charges" in art. 62, II, for the purpose of working hours, and the framework depends on factual elements of the employment relationship (BRASIL, 1943, art. 62, II). A system permission does not characterize management position, employer representation or equivalence between agent and employee. The analogy also does not shift responsibility to the agent: a model has no patrimony, does not submit to organizational sanctions and does not become preplaced for being described as "team member". The legal categories apply to human and organizational participants, according to the facts, duties and the incident regime.

4. Who actually receives the delegation?

Proposal for an article: socio-technical delegation of authority. The organization does not delegate to an isolated model. It configures a structure composed of:

  • model and version;
  • instructions, policies and business rules;
  • context, memory and input data;
  • orchestrator and planning mechanism;
  • runtime and execution environment;
  • identity, credentials and scope;
  • tools, APIs and external systems;
  • mechanisms of observability, approval and containment.

Organization → Agentic system → Running layer → Real World effects.

The organization defines the goal; the agency system interprets and selects steps; the execution layer transforms choices into calls to tools and APIs; the effects change data, messages, contracts or infrastructure.

The architecture requires separating three layers of authorization, which may coincide but are not assumed from each other:

  • Technical permission: the possibility of carrying out an operation.
  • Organisational authorisation: the internal decision to allow the operation in that context.
  • Legal authorisation: which arises from competence, contract, representation, law and other requirements.

Known controls. The principle of lesser privilege determines that each program and each user operate with the smallest set of privileges required for the task (SALTZER; SCHROEDER, 1975). RBAC associates permissions to roles assigned to users. ABAC decides the authorization by evaluating attributes of the subject, object, requested operation and, in some cases, the environment (HU et al., 2014). The segregation of functions separates incompatible activities. These controls are technical authorization mechanisms; they do not define office, personality or legal power.

Interpretation applied to the case. In PocketOS, an account scope token, stored in a file other than the task, allowed an execution linked to staging achieve a destructive operation on a production volume (ABDELWAHAB, 2026; CRANE, 2026). The issue of governance is why architecture allowed a task assigned to an environment to reach another environment and an irreversible operation without independent barrier. The credential exceeded the purpose of the task, contrary to the smallest privilege; there was a lack of a policy to assess the attribute "environment" and the irreversibility of the operation. Railway itself concluded that agents should use surfaces designed for them, not a raw endpoint accessed by a forgotten token in a configuration file (ABDELWAHAB, 2026).

Chain of participants. Organization, architecture, implementation, configuration, operation and suppliers occupy different roles, and each role can generate different duties (section 6.1). To participate technically is not enough to establish legal liability for any damage.

5. A matrix to govern autonomy

Proposal for an article. The following matrix is contribution of this article; it is not recognized standard, validated method or legal obligation. Yeah. non-compensatory: the dimensions do not add up to an average score, and an excellent result in competence does not compensate for the absence of legitimate authority or the inability to contain a system of high criticality.

SizeMain questionPossible evidence
1. Operational competenceHas the system demonstrated reliable performance in this task and in this context?Representative tests, error rate, robustness, known limits, revalidation
2. Operational autonomyHow much do you operate without intervention?Duration, initiative, triggers, number of decisions and actions without approval, type of supervision
3. Elbow and authorityWhat appeals, decisions and effects does politics authorize?Identity, scope, environment, financial, data and communication limits, irreversibility, required approval
4. Criticality and impactWhat happens if the action fails or is undue?Financial, operational, legal, social, reputational and rights damage; scale; reversibility
5. GovernanceCan the organization enforce the limits and observe, audit, interrupt, recover and respond?Enforcement policies, records, provenance, containment, rollback, reconstruction of the action and its authorisation

Condition A — Legitimacy of the delegation. Does the organization have legal, contractual, financial and institutional authority to delegate the activity? She may authorize an agent to prepare a minute, but she may not be able to delegate, without additional controls, a decision subject to regulatory approval, contractual representation or processing of sensitive data.

Condition B — Governance capacity. Can the organization observe, audit, interrupt and respond to the consequences?

Elbow (dimension 3) and governability (dimension 5) are distinct. The handle belongs to the normative design: what the policy states that the agent can do. Governance belongs to the technical and operational capacity: how the organization prevents the agent from going beyond the scope and how it limits, interrupts or reverses failures. It requires connecting each action to an identity, a credentials, a policy, a context, a version and a permit, and being able to revoke access, interrupt the operation and recover effects when possible.

The organisation shall not grant a measure extending beyond its real capacity to govern the effects of the agent's actions.

Decision flow: need → competence and criticality → definition of heave → legitimacy (Condition A) → governability (Condition B) → limited authorization, reduction of permissions or not authorization → monitoring and reassessment.

Competence comes early because it is a condition of eligibility; without it demonstrated in the context, the flow to. Criticality comes together because it defines the rigor of the following steps. If Condition The failure, the answer is not to authorize. If Condition B failure, the answer is to reduce the handle to the governing point or not to authorize.

Technical example. A development agent can read production records to diagnose a failure, write code in a test repository and open a pull request. This does not authorize you to exclude banks, change administrative credentials, modify access controls or execute irreversible migrations. A configuration consistent with the matrix could include:

  • short-term reading credentials restricted to production diagnostic resources;
  • writing credentials valid only in the test environment;
  • authorisation policy that evaluates environment and type of operation and denies by default destructive operations outside the test environment;
  • exclusion postponed or reversible in the service itself, regardless of the instruction given to the staff member;
  • backups outside the failed radius of the protected resource;
  • mandatory human approval for critical changes.

The goal is to align the handle to the possible effect of the action, not approve each generated line.

Revalidation. The demonstrated competence can no longer be used when changing the model, tools, environment or policy. Autonomy should decrease when observability or containment are degraded.

6. Who answers for the consequences?

6.1 Layers of responsibility

Interpretation. Responsibility can be analyzed in layers:

  • Institutional: decision to use, purpose, acceptance of risks and controls.
  • Architecture: permissions, separation of environments, barriers and containment.
  • Implementation: code defects, integration or configuration.
  • Operational: concrete authorization, monitoring and response.
  • From suppliers: contract, service, defect, information provided, exercised control and causal link.

The layers indicate where duties may arise; they do not themselves establish the responsibility of any participant.

6.2 Brazilian law in force

Civil Code. Art. 186 defines unlawful act as the violation of law that causes harm to others, by action or voluntary omission, negligence or recklessness; art. 187 deals with the abuse of law. Art. 927, caput, obliges to repair those who cause damage by unlawful act; the single paragraph provides for the obligation to repair independently of guilt in cases specified in law or when the activity normally carried out by the perpetrator of the damage entails, by its nature, risk to the rights of others (BRASIL, 2002, Arts. 186, 187 and 927).

Interpretation. The use of agents with operational autonomy and the ability to produce destructive effects in critical systems may contribute to characterize, in the concrete case, risk activity in accordance with the single paragraph of article 927, especially with high exposure, irreversibility, control asymmetry or damage predictability. The conclusion is not due to the mere presence of AI. Even recognized the framework, objective responsibility dispenses the proof of guilt, but not that of damage and nexus, neither excludes the exclusions and the contribution of other participants.

Articles 932, III, and 933 hold the employer or principal responsible for the acts of employees, servants and pre-employees in or on account of the work, even if without self-guilty (BRASIL, 2002, articles 932, III, and 933). Limit of analogy: these devices do not make an AI agent employed or posed. They may focus on the act of a person in such categories, as the professional who configured or operated the system, according to the facts. The absence of human intervention alone does not determine objective responsibility.

LGPD. The law applies when personal data are processed. Article 20 gives to the data subject the right to request the review of decisions made solely on the basis of automated processing of personal data that affect their interests, including those that define their personal, professional, consumer and credit profile or aspects of their personality; §1o obliges the controller to provide, when requested, clear information on criteria and procedures, observed the commercial and industrial secrets (BRASIL, 2018, art. 20, as amended by Law No. 13,853/2019). The current wording does not require review by natural person in all automation: the right depends solely on automated decision affecting interests of the data subject, and on request.

Article 42 obliges the controller or the operator who, in the processing of personal data, causes damage in violation of the legislation to repair it. The operator responds jointly when the law or legal instructions of the controller are broken; controllers directly involved also respond jointly; and the judge may reverse the burden of proof in favor of of the data subject when the claim is verossimile, there is hyposufficiency or the proof is excessively costly (BRASIL, 2018, art. 42, §§ 1 and 2). Article 43 provides for exclusions, and Article 46 requires technical and administrative security measures from the design of the product or service (BRASIL, 2018, Articles 43 and 46, §2o). Interpretation: these devices do not transform all AI failure into indemnable damage, but make governance, security, instructions and legally relevant records when the event involves personal data.

CDC. The Consumer Protection Code may apply when there is a consumer relationship. Art. 12 holds manufacturers, producers, manufacturers and importers responsible for product defects, and Art. 14 blames the service provider, regardless of guilt, for defects in delivery; the service is defective when it does not provide the safety that the consumer can expect (BRASIL, 1990, Arts. 12 and 14, §1o). Art. 17 equates all victims of the event to consumers, and art. 25, §1o, establishes solidarity among those responsible for the damage (BRASIL, 1990, Arts 17 and 25, §1o). The incidence is not automatic in relation to business, hiring API or internal use.

Civil Marco from the Internet. The article did not identify concrete relevance and does not examine it.

6.3 Brazilian legislative proposal

The PL 2.338/2023 was presented in the Senate on May 3, 2023, approved by the Senate in December 2024 and referred to the House of Representatives on March 17, 2025 (NATIONAL CONGRESS, 2025). On November 21, 2026, the House record records the situation "awaiting the opinion of the rapporteur in the Special Committee on Artificial Intelligence", a system of priority and appreciation by the Plenary (CAMARA DOS DEPUTES, 2026). The project It's not law; its text indicates legislative policy and can change.

6.4 European Union: AI Act

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 defines AI system as a system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and distinguishes supplier (provider) responsible for the implementation (deployer) (EUROPEAN UNION, 2024, Art. 3, 1, 3 and 4). Article 2 defines the scope, and the rules vary according to the risk and role of the operator; the regulation does not apply indistinctly to any system.

For high-risk systems, three groups of devices relate to the thesis:

  • Human supervision (Art. 14): See section 2.
  • Records (Articles 12, 19 and 26, §6o): automatic event recording; o deployer keep the records under your control for at least six months, except for different legal disposition.
  • Duties deployer (Art. 26): use the system as instructed; assign supervision to natural persons with competence, training and authority necessary, in addition to the necessary support; monitor the operation and suspend use when there is suspicion of risk (UNION EUROPEAN, 2026, art. 26, §§ 1, 2, 5 and 6).

Interpretation. Art. 26, §2o, requires the supervisor to have authority, not just presence. It is the distinction between nominal presence and effective ability to intervene that this article defends.

Temporal applicability. The Regulation entered into force on 1 August 2024, with staggered application in Article 113 (EUROPEAN UNION, 2024). Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), of 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and in force since 27 July 2026, amended the schedule (UNION EUROPEAN, 2026). According to law firms (secondary sources), high-risk obligations became valid on 2 December 2027 for the systems of Annex III and on 2 August 2028 for systems integrated into Annex I products (WHITE & CASE, 2026; CUTRECASAS, 2026). At the cut date, therefore, the obligations of Articles 12, 14 and 26 for high risk exist in the normative text, but do not yet apply. The consolidated version of EUR-Lex has no legal effect; the authentic texts are those of the Official Journal (UNION EUROPEAN, 2026).

6.5 Voluntary frameworks and technical standards

  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework: published on January 26, 2023, of voluntary use, organized in the functions Government, Map, Measure and Manage; the official page states that it is under review (NIST, 2023). It may serve as evidence of diligence, but it creates no legal obligation.
  • OECD principles for AI: Intergovernmental recommendation adopted in 2019 and revised on 3 May 2024 (OECD, 2024). It provides for agency capacity and human supervision (principle 1.2, b); mechanisms to safely undo, repair or disable systems that risk causing undue damage (1.4, b); and traceability of data sets, processes and decisions throughout the life cycle (1.5, b). It's not directly coercive law.
  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023: technical standard published in December 2023 (1st edition), which specifies requirements to establish, implement, maintain and continuously improve an AI management system for organisations that provide or use AI-based products and services (ISO, 2023). It does not replace law or proof of causality; a certification does not prove no responsibility.

6.6 Comparative cases

Except PocketOS, the following cases no involve agentic systems; illustrate organizational responsibility for automation.

  • Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149). On 14 February 2024, the Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia ruled a small-case dispute over incorrect information given by the company's chatbot regarding mourning tariffs. The court called "notable" the thesis that chatbot would be separate legal entity and stated that the company accounts for all the information on its website (par. 27); concluded that it did not take reasonable care with the accuracy of chatbot (par. 28), recognized negligent misrepresentation (par. 32) and fixed a total conviction of CAD 812.02 (par. 44) (CIVIL RESOLUTION COURT, 2024). The decision has no general binding effect nor does it deal with autonomous agents.
  • EEOC v. iTutorGroup (2023). On September 11, 2023, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), a federal agency in the United States, reported an agreement of US$ 365 thousand in action in which it claimed that the company’s application software automatically rejected women aged 55 years or older and men aged 60 years or older, reaching more than 200 candidates (EEOC, 2023). The statement describes triage software configured with a rule, not a generative AI or agent.
  • Robodebt (Australia). The report of the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme was presented on 7 July 2023. Recommendation 17.1 proposes legislative reform to create a consistent legal framework for automation in government services; 17.2 proposes an agency to monitor and audit automated decisions (ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME, 2023). Robodebt was administrative automation, not an agency system; it shows that automating does not eliminate requirements of legality, review and institutional responsibility.
  • PocketOS (2026). See section 1; there was no judicial decision on liability.

Joint interpretation. In the first three cases, the organization did not remove its duties by placing an automated system between itself and third parties. PocketOS adds the agentic element: the system performed an action that no one had ordered.

7. The limits of the proposal

7.1 Counterarguments

Probabilistic and context-dependent competence. Model performance varies with task, data and environment; a test cannot become license for autonomy. The matrix requires revalidation and criticality analysis, but does not offer universal numerical threshold.

Legitimate autonomy in low-risk activities. The objection proceeds. In reversible and low-impact tasks, the organization can use further supervision, cost limits, narrow scopes, sampling and automated containment. The requirement is proportionality, not constant intervention.

Unfeasible to approve each action. When an agent performs hundreds of actions per task, individual approval tends to become automatic ratification. The matrix shifts control to the handle and governability: reduce what can be done and make reversible what is done.

Automation biases. Parasuraman and Manzey (2010) show that complacency with automation appears in lay participants and specialists, does not resolve with simple practice, and that automation bias produces omission errors and commission when decision aid is imperfect. A pressured supervisor without information or authority can only ratify the exit. The matrix treats supervision as a combination of understanding, attention, competence, authority, observability and ability to interrupt.

Record limits, explicability, shutdown and reversibility. A record shows that a call occurred, but does not prove that the authorization was legitimate, that the context was correct or that the recorded justification was not produced later. The text generated by the agent in the PocketOS case has a form of explanation, but it is not evidence of the cause. An emergency shutdown interrupts new actions without undoing already outsourced effects. The OECD recommends traceability, and the AI Act requires records in high-risk systems, but neither guarantees perfect causal reconstruction (OECD, 2024; EUROPEAN UNION, 2024).

Sufficientness of traditional mechanisms. RBAC, ABAC, lower privilege, function segregation, change management and production controls can suffice in several contexts. PocketOS can be read as a failure of classic controls (token scope, backups in the same radius of failure, deletion without delay), not something unique from the AI. The matrix does not replace these mechanisms; it asks if they cover initiative, tool selection, planning and operation duration of an agent, including the possibility of the system looking for and using a credentials that no one has given it for that task.

Excessive responsibility of technical professionals. Architects and developers do not automatically respond for any consequence of a system. The analysis considers who had control, what information he had, what duties he assumed, what risks were predictable, what warnings were given and what the causal contribution of each participant was.

7.2 Limitations

  • The proposal is conceptual and has not been empirically validated.
  • The matrix does not offer universal numerical thresholds.
  • The analogy with people management is functional, not labor.
  • The article does not state any participant's automatic responsibility.
  • The proposal depends on faulty identity, authorisation, audit and containment technologies, especially in multi-agent systems.
  • Public evidence on incidents of agents in production is fragmented; in the PocketOS case, part of the facts comes from statements by the parties, and the authorship of the consulted copy of the founder's account was not confirmed.

7.3 Conditions for rebuttal or revision

The matrix shall be reviewed or rejected if:

  1. does not produce better decisions than traditional risk authorisation and management mechanisms;
  2. existing mechanisms adequately resolve certain contexts;
  3. the dimension of autonomy does not add relevant information to the risk assessment in certain scenarios;
  4. its operation in multiagent systems generate costs and ambiguities higher than benefits.

7.4 Search Agenda

  • test scenarios and simulations that compare decisions with and without the matrix, and comparison with RBAC, ABAC and traditional change management;
  • case studies and systematic analysis of incidents of agents in production, including explicit raising reduce incidents;
  • comparison of HITL, HOTL and HOOTL in tasks of different criticalities;
  • evidence of records and provenance;
  • treatment by the brazilian courts of causality, contracts, records and distributed responsibility.

8. Responsibility is not automatic

The central question was how an organization can delegate authority to a non-human entity without unduly delegating its own responsibility. The answer has six parts:

  1. Autonomy extends operational delegation and, with it, the need to define where the action is legitimate.
  2. Technical capacity does not equal legitimate authority. Being able to execute does not authorize to execute.
  3. Technical permissions may exceed the purpose of the task. In PocketOS, an account scope credential has achieved production from a job of staging, without the sources allowing to blame a specific participant.
  4. Moist and governability come before deployment. The organization should not grant greater heave than it can govern.
  5. Withdrawing the human from execution does not extinguish duties; changes the form of supervision.
  6. Legal imputation depends on the facts and the regime. In Brazil: Civil Code, LGPD, CDC, contract, sector legislation or combination between them. PL 2.338/2023 is not yet law.

Agents should not be treated as employees. Organizations may use competence, attribution, responsibility and supervision to design technical governance, provided that they do not import labor relations or confuse credentials with representation. Competence is a condition of eligibility; authorization depends on legitimacy, criticality and governability.

An organization can delegate tasks, decisions and operational autonomy. It cannot be assumed that the transfer of execution to an artificial system would transfer the legitimacy of the decision or eliminate its own duties.

In short

To whom the company delegates when delegating to the AI

An organization can delegate tasks and operational autonomy to an AI agent, but cannot assume that the technical delegation transfers legitimate authority or liability. Technical capacity is not authority: being able to execute does not authorize to execute.

  • The PocketOS case (2026) — in a routine task in the test environment, an agent found a large, forgotten credential and erased the production bank; the data was recovered later.
  • Five dimensions, no average — competence, autonomy, height, criticality and governability; an excellent result in one does not compensate for failure in another.
  • No greater than governability — the organisation must not grant a higher level than it can observe, interrupt and reverse.
  • The machine does not respond — the imputation depends on the facts and the regime; in Brazil, Civil Code, LGPD and CDC, and PL 2.338/2023 is not yet law.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in the PocketOS case?

On April 24, 2026, a programming agent performing a routine task in the staging environment excluded, with an account scope token found in the user's machine, the volume containing the PocketOS production database. Volume level backups were in the same volume. Railway reported after they recovered the data and started applying a 48-hour postponement.

What's the difference between competence and authority?

Competence is demonstrated in the context, with known limits. Authority is the institutional or legal power to decide, approve, represent or produce an effect. Competence is a condition of eligibility, not automatic authorization.

What are the five dimensions of the matrix?

Operational competence, operational autonomy, responsibility and authority, criticality and impact, and governability. The matrix is non-compensatory and is subject to two conditions: legitimacy of delegation and governance capacity. It is a proposal of the article, without empirical validation.

Who answers when an AI agent does damage?

The system doesn't answer for itself. Responsibility can involve institutional, architectural, implementation, operational and supplier layers, and depends on the applicable regime, conduct, damage and causal link. In Brazil there is no specific regime for AI agents; PL 2.338/2023 continues to be processed.
